extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, philosophers of science, and mathematicians interested in the nature of mathematical explanation
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of what counts as a mathematical explanation (including explanatory proofs and explanatory non-proofs), with attention to conditions, mechanisms, generalizability, and distinctions between explanation and mere proof or coincidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory proof exploits shared respects across cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof explains a result exactly when the proof 'exploits some other respect in which those cases are alike and from there arrives at the result by treating all of the cases in the same way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation is tied to showing a structural or relational feature common to cases that yields the result; example: the proof that every 'calculator number' is divisible by 37 explains why the divisibility is not coincidental. If a proof merely shows truth without pointing to such a shared respect, it fails to explain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical explanations can be non-proofs (explanatory non-proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are mathematical arguments that are not proofs but nevertheless explain; the paper addresses what it would take for a non-proof to explain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper focuses on a concrete example (an argument about the derivative of an infinite sum of differentiable functions) that mathematicians regard as explanatory despite not being a proof. Contrast with work that focuses on non-arguments that nonetheless explain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory status depends on further conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument 'may explain—but may not. As we will see, the explanation requires certain further conditions to be satisfied.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an argument explains can hinge on mathematical hypotheses (e.g., uniform convergence when interchanging derivative and infinite sum). Identifying and checking these further conditions is part of assessing explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism identification as hallmark of explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanation often uncovers the 'crucial mechanism involved in the situation'—the feature that accounts for why the phenomenon holds or fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited pedagogical language: 'Specific counter-examples ... do not contribute to the understanding of the general case. On the other hand, general examples uncover the crucial mechanism.' Explanatory arguments should reveal mechanisms rather than merely listing instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: General examples vs. specific counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific counter-examples merely refute a statement; general examples provide understanding by showing the mechanism, and thus have explanatory power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: relying on single counterexamples to claim understanding. Apply this to cases such as the sum rule failing for infinite series: a specific counterexample refutes but a general example that reveals the mechanism explains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation by showing why a proof does not generalize
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanatory non-proof can explain 'why a given proof in the finite case does not carry over to the infinite case' by identifying the obstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than proving the explanandum, an explanatory non-proof may illuminate the barrier to generalization (e.g., what additional property is missing in the infinite case). This counts as explanatory when the salient contrast is between finite and infinite cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salience and mathematical coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a result's salient feature is that it identifies a respect in which various cases are alike, then a proof explains the result when it appeals to another respect in which those cases are alike; absent such an explanation the result may be a 'mathematical coincidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to distinguish genuine explanations from coincidences: explanatory proofs trace the likeness that produces the result; if no such likeness is identified, the apparent pattern may be accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanations must identify relevant differences, not merely note scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles that only state scope (e.g., 'this holds for finite but not infinite') without specifying the relevant difference fail to explain: 'The principle of mathematical induction ... does not specify any difference between the finite and infinite cases (other than that the latter is infinite) that is standing in the way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good explanations point to the substantive property that blocks or enables generalization; merely naming the excluded domain is insufficient for explanatory content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability as a contested requirement for explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement that an explanatory proof must generalize (as in Steiner's account) is disputed; some examples (e.g., certain proofs of the IVT) may explain without generalizing to other domains like the rationals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of explanatory worth may disagree on whether generalizability is necessary. The paper uses examples and literature (e.g., Resnik & Kushner) to argue that Steiner's generalizability criterion may be too strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope delimitation of 'mathematical explanation' used in discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper restricts 'mathematical explanation' to the sense prevalent in recent literature: explanations that bear on why mathematical facts are true (distinct from pedagogical or how-to explanations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly exclude other senses (e.g., classroom explanations of 'how to evaluate an integral' or 'what uniform convergence means') from the target notion. This delimitation guides what counts as explanatory in the paper's arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory remarks can account for differences in problem difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanatory account may show 'why one problem turns out to be so much more difficult than another, seemingly closely related one' by pointing to methodological or structural reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Hardy's remark explaining why odd cases are harder than even cases by showing what makes the odd case lack the simplifying structure; such remarks have explanatory value in clarifying comparative difficulty.
